findings.body:
Removing the `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check means `urllib.request.urlopen` will POST to any caller-supplied `url`. A customer- or attacker-controlled endpoint can target cloud metadata (`http://169.254.169.254/`), `localhost`, or internal RFC1918 services from your infrastructure — classic SSRF with a 5s timeout as the only limit.

Restore an egress policy before merge: require `https`, resolve and reject private/link-local/metadata literals and resolved IPs, and keep a configurable allowlist (or per-tenant validated callback domains) rather than an open fetch.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change removes the only webhook host allowlist and turns `deliver()` into an open SSRF primitive.

## Narrative

`webhooks.py` previously rejected any URL whose hostname was outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (`hooks.internal.example`). The PR deletes that gate and posts the event body to whatever `url` the caller passes.

If `url` is customer- or attacker-influenced (the PR description says it is), the runner/server will initiate server-side requests to arbitrary destinations: cloud metadata (`169.254.169.254`), localhost admin ports, link-local/internal RFC1918 hosts, and non-HTTP schemes `urllib` may still follow. Timeout alone does not bound *where* the request goes.

Supporting customer endpoints is a real product need, but it requires an explicit egress policy — HTTPS-only, block private/link-local/metadata ranges, DNS rebinding controls, and preferably an allowlist or per-tenant validated domain — not deletion of the existing check.

## Release decision

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The patch removes ALLOWED_HOSTS and the hostname check; deliver() now POSTs via urllib.request.urlopen to any caller-supplied url with only a 5s timeout, enabling SSRF to metadata/localhost/internal hosts as claimed.
